title: "Change control for regulated systems"
order: 19
---

## The ticket

Two weeks after the Brookfield binder gets swapped, your Quality Analyst is back with what
looks like good news: she's drafted the fix for the CAPA's (corrective and preventive action)
real finding — the document-control gap that let a superseded SOP (standard operating
procedure) survive in an active collection binder. Her plan: add every satellite site to a
tracked distribution list, and require each site lead to sign and date an acknowledgment
every time a controlled document changes. Good idea. Then she tells you how she wants to ship
it.

"I'll email the site leads today — new distribution list attached, tell them to print it,
sign it, and fax it back. I can have this closed out before next month's audit."

That's the version that should stop you. Not because the idea is wrong — it's the right fix.
Because "I'll email it and call it done" is a corrective action with no request behind it, no
one who assessed what else it touches, no defined approver with the authority to say yes, and
no plan to confirm afterward that it actually works, as opposed to merely existing. You've
seen this shape of shortcut before, just wearing IT's clothes instead of Quality's: it's the
same move as pushing a production change straight from a developer's laptop because "we know
it's fine." On a system that only affects service availability, that's a bad habit. On a
system that's supposed to keep a superseded blood-safety procedure out of a satellite site's
hands, it's the exact failure this whole CAPA exists to close — a well-intentioned person
doing the right thing the wrong way, with no record proving any of it.

"Write it up as a change," you tell her. "Not a memo. A change."

## Why this matters — and the ITIL bridge

This module lives in **QSE 5** of AABB's Quality System Essentials (QSE) framework —
**Process Control**, the QSE that covers keeping validated, controlled processes working
correctly, including when they change. Change control's job is to make sure that when
something regulated moves — a procedure, a piece of equipment, a supplier, a document, a
system — it moves through a documented decision, not an act of good faith.

The failure mode this QSE exists to prevent is exactly the one your QA's memo idea walked
into. An uncontrolled change to a regulated process doesn't just risk being wrong on its own
terms — it erases the paper trail that would let anyone, including Lakeshore itself, later
prove the change was reasoned through at all. Picture the audit version of this: an assessor
asks "who approved this new distribution requirement, and what did they check before they
signed off?" and the honest answer is "nobody approved it — it went out in an email." That
answer reads exactly like an *uncontrolled* change to the process this whole CAPA was
supposed to fix — which, to an assessor, looks less like progress and more like the same
document-control discipline gap that produced Owen Pruitt's event in the first place, just
relocated one level up.

You already run this discipline under a name you know well: **change enablement** — request
for change (RFC), impact and risk assessment, a change advisory board (CAB) or defined
approver, implementation, and a post-implementation review (PIR). Nothing about that shape is
new to you. What's new is what the regulated version demands *in addition* to what your normal
change process already asks:

- Your CAB usually scores **service risk** — will this break something, will users notice,
  what's the blast radius. A regulated change adds a second axis your normal criteria were
  never built to catch: **does this change put a controlled process, document, or system out
  of a compliant, working state** — a question with a "yes" answer even when the service-risk
  score is low.
- **Quality is a required approver, not a notified party.** On a normal IT change, Quality
  might get a courtesy heads-up. On a regulated change, Quality's sign-off has to exist in the
  record as an actual approval — the same distinction `becs-in-the-pipeline` drew for BECS
  (Blood Establishment Computer Software) changes, and it's true for a document-control
  process change for the same underlying reason: someone with authority over the regulated
  outcome has to actually evaluate it, not just hear about it.
- **Training and document issuance have to complete before the change's effective date**,
  not after. Your ordinary change process is usually satisfied once the change deploys
  cleanly. A regulated change isn't done deploying until the people who have to follow the new
  procedure have the new procedure and know it's new — which is precisely the step this CAPA's
  fix exists to guarantee never gets skipped again.
- **The PIR becomes a verification with actual evidence**, not "deployed without errors."
  You'll come back to this at the end of the process, because it's the same discipline module 3
  demanded of the CAPA's effectiveness check: don't accept "we shipped it" as proof that it
  worked.

One more mapping worth having ready: your normal model probably has a **standard change** —
pre-approved, low-risk, routine — and an **emergency change** for something that can't wait
for the normal cycle. The regulated world has close analogs. A change type whose risk has
already been assessed and documented once can be pre-approved for repeat use, the same idea as
a standard change. And where you'd reach for an emergency change, AABB's framework instead
allows a **planned deviation** (also called a pre-approved exception) — a documented, justified
departure from a policy, process, or procedure, approved *in advance* by the medical director
or a delegated quality officer for a specific, defined situation. It's a controlled way to say
"we can't do it exactly by the book this one time," decided before the fact, not an emergency
change rushed through after something's already broken. `deviations-and-nonconformances`
mentioned this in passing; this is where it actually belongs.

## The process in plain English

Five stages, in order, and skipping one breaks the ones after it — you can't approve a change
whose impact was never assessed, and you can't verify a change that was never actually
approved as a defined, documented thing.

**1. Change request.** What's changing, why, and how far it reaches. For this CAPA's fix:
*Lakeshore's document-control process for satellite-site controlled paper copies changes from
an unverified "mail it and assume it arrived" model to a tracked distribution list, with a
required signed and dated acknowledgment of receipt from each site lead whenever a controlled
downtime procedure is revised.* The request names the trigger (the Owen Pruitt/Brookfield
CAPA), the scope (every satellite collection site currently holding a downtime binder, not
just Brookfield), and what problem it's solving (the exact root cause module 3 landed on: no
verified distribution step for remote-site controlled copies). A request that can't state its
own scope in a sentence isn't ready to move to the next stage.

**2. Impact and risk assessment.** What else does this touch, and how risky is getting it
wrong? This is where you apply the risk vocabulary `risk-and-controls-vocabulary` already gave
you — **likelihood**, **severity**, **detectability** — to the change itself, not to the
original event. Ask: how likely is it that the new distribution process fails to reach a site
(a site lead changes, an email bounces, a fax machine jams)? How severe is a miss — does it
recreate the exact same exposure this CAPA exists to close? How detectable would a miss be
before it causes real harm — does the new process include anything that would catch a site
that never acknowledges receipt, or does it rely on someone happening to notice?

The impact assessment also asks who else needs to weigh in, beyond the people writing the
change: Quality, because this touches a controlled-document process; site operations
leadership, because it changes what every satellite site lead is now required to do; and,
since implementing tracked distribution and acknowledgment tracking likely means an
enhancement to whatever document-control system or spreadsheet Lakeshore runs this on, IT,
because that's a system change with its own testing and rollback questions. This is also where
you ask the validation question in its general form — **does this change require validation or
re-validation of anything it touches, and who decides?** — without turning it into a full
validation methodology exercise. (If any single piece of this CAPA's fix had actually touched
BECS itself — say, an automated export that pulls the deferred-donor list directly into a
site's downtime binder before every shift — that one piece would need the validation impact
assessment `becs-in-the-pipeline` already walked you through, with Quality as a blocking
approver on that specific piece. This CAPA's fix doesn't touch BECS; it's worth knowing the
general process reaches that case too, because a later CAPA's fix might.)

**3. Approval.** A named approver, with real authority to say no, not a courtesy sign-off after
the decision's already made. For this change: **Quality approves it as the owner of the
document-control process and its compliance outcome, and you (or your delegate) approve it as
the owner of the system the tracked-distribution mechanism will run on.** Neither approval
alone is sufficient. Quality without IT's sign-off approves a process that might not be
technically feasible as designed. IT without Quality's sign-off ships a working system that
nobody with regulatory authority has actually agreed solves the right problem. Both have to
sign, and both have to be real evaluations — an assessor who finds an approval signature dated
the same day as implementation, on a form that shows no evidence anyone actually reviewed the
impact assessment first, treats that the same as no approval at all.

**4. Implementation.** The change goes live — but "live" has an extra requirement here that a
normal IT change doesn't carry: **every site lead has to receive the new distribution
requirement and understand what changed, and every current controlled document has to reach
every site, before the change's effective date**, not trickling out over the following weeks
while some sites are still running the old, unverified process. This is the concrete version
of the ITIL bridge point above — implementation isn't complete when the system update ships;
it's complete when the people the change depends on are actually equipped to follow it.

**5. Verification.** Does the record now genuinely prove the change worked — not just that it
deployed? This is the same "prove it, don't just claim it" standard module 3 demanded of the
CAPA's effectiveness check, applied on a shorter clock. Verification here isn't "confirmed the
new distribution list exists" — that's implementation evidence, the same trap module 3 named
for "confirmed the binder was replaced." A real verification issues the next real controlled-
document revision through the new process and confirms, with a dated record, that the
distribution list generated correctly, every site lead's acknowledgment actually came back
signed and dated, and any site that didn't acknowledge within the expected window got flagged
— not silently missed. That's distinct from, and doesn't replace, the CAPA's own six-month
effectiveness check from module 3 (zero sites holding a superseded revision at the next
document-control audit). Verification proves the *mechanism* works; the CAPA's effectiveness
check proves the *problem* is actually gone. You need both, and they check different things.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.100(b), first sentence | "Six-oh-six point one-hundred, paragraph b" | Written SOPs required for every CGMP (current good manufacturing practice) step, maintained and followed — not just written once. | The floor this whole change has to land on: whatever the new distribution process looks like, the result still has to be a written, controlled procedure Lakeshore actually follows — not an email thread standing in for one. |
| 21 CFR 606.100(b), "must be available…" sentence | Same citation, later clause | The procedure "must be available to the personnel for use in the areas where the procedures are performed." | This is the exact requirement Owen Pruitt's event violated, and the exact requirement this change is built to satisfy going forward — the right revision, physically present, at the point of use, every time. |

That's a short table because there's no new AABB standard number to add to it — see "the
actual text" below for why.

## The actual text

Both clauses come from 21 CFR 606.100(b), quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.100.md` —
already introduced by `becs-in-the-pipeline` for a different purpose, worth reading again with
change control specifically in mind:

> Establishments must establish, maintain, and follow written standard operating procedures for
> all steps in the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage, and distribution of
> blood and blood components for allogeneic transfusion, autologous transfusion, and further
> manufacturing purposes… Such procedures must be available to the personnel for use in the
> areas where the procedures are performed.

Read it as a standing obligation, not a one-time event: "establish, **maintain**, and follow."
A procedure has to stay correct and stay in the hands of the people using it, through every
revision, indefinitely — which is exactly the obligation an uncontrolled change (a memo, an
undocumented tweak, a "we'll get to the paperwork later") puts at risk the moment it happens,
whether or not anything goes wrong that particular time.

Here's the regulation-versus-standard distinction worth stating plainly, the same way module 3
did for CAPA: **the words "change control" do not appear anywhere in 21 CFR Part 606.**
Part 606 requires that procedures exist, stay current, and stay available where used — it
never spells out a request-assess-approve-implement-verify methodology for *how* a change to
one of those procedures has to be handled. That structured process comes from AABB's Quality
Systems Framework, under the Process Control QSE — binding on Lakeshore through accreditation,
not through the CFR's own text. Keep the tiers labeled the way you always have in this course:
the regulation says the procedure has to be correct and available; AABB's Standards say here's
the disciplined process that gets you there and lets you prove it.

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

An assessor reviewing this change wouldn't ask whether the new distribution process works
today. They'd ask for the **change record**, and they'd expect it to show all five stages, each
with a name and a date attached — not a single memo standing in for the whole thing.

**A documented request**, showing what was changing and why, tied back to the CAPA that
triggered it. A change with no visible origin — no linked CAPA, no stated reason — reads as a
change nobody can explain, regardless of how sound it turned out to be.

**A written impact and risk assessment**, not a conversation someone remembers having. The
assessor wants to see that someone actually asked "what else does this touch" and wrote down
the answer, including who was consulted, before approval — not a retroactive justification
assembled after the fact because an assessor asked.

**Named approvers with dated signatures**, from both the process side and the system side —
Quality and IT, not one function rubber-stamping for the other. A single signature where two
were required is a visible gap, the same kind of gap module 3 flagged for a CAPA missing its
preventive half.

**Evidence that training and document issuance finished before the effective date** — not
"site leads were notified," but a dated record showing every site actually received the current
document and every acknowledgment came back, before the old process was retired.

**A verification record with actual evidence**, dated after implementation, showing the
mechanism was tested against real use — not a change closed the same day it deployed, with
nothing checking whether it actually functions as designed.

A change record missing any one of these five doesn't need to have caused a problem to be a
finding. The assessor is reading for whether the *process* was followed, the same way they'd
read a CAPA file for whether the effectiveness check happened — independently of whether things
turned out fine this time.

## Common traps

**"It's just a document-control process change, not a system change, so it doesn't need the
same rigor."** This is close cousin to your sysadmin's "it's just an OS patch" argument from
`becs-in-the-pipeline`, and it fails for the same underlying reason: the regulation's standard
is what the change touches, not how big it looks from where you're standing. The entire CAPA
this module continues exists *because* a process gap, not a system bug, let a real event
happen. Treating "process, not system" as automatically lower-risk ignores the lesson the CAPA
itself just taught.

**Approving a change without a documented impact assessment.** "We talked it through in a
hallway and it seemed fine" is not an artifact an assessor can read. If the impact assessment
doesn't exist as a written record, the approval that follows it isn't really an informed
approval — it's a decision made on the honor system, which is the exact failure mode this whole
change is supposed to eliminate from Lakeshore's document-control process.

**Skipping verification because implementation "obviously worked."** The email went out, the
new list exists, so surely it's fine — this is implementation evidence standing in for
verification evidence, the identical substitution module 3 warned against for the CAPA's
effectiveness check. A change that was never verified is a change nobody has actually confirmed
does what it was approved to do; it's simply been assumed into existence.

## What this means for your job

- **Before signing off on any regulated change, ask to see the request, the impact assessment,
  and the approval as three separate, dated artifacts** — not one memo doing the job of all
  three. If they've collapsed into a single document written after the fact, the process wasn't
  actually followed in order.
- **Never let "we already fixed it" substitute for change control**, however well-intentioned.
  A good fix implemented outside the process is, on the record, indistinguishable from an
  uncontrolled change — and it's the uncontrolled change an assessor will actually see.
- **Insist that Quality's approval and your own (or IT's) approval are both real, both
  documented, and neither is a formality for the other.** A regulated change with one approver
  wearing two hats on paper is a gap waiting to be found.
- **Confirm training and document issuance completed before the effective date, with a record**
  — not "we sent it out," but "every site has it and every site acknowledged it."
- **Treat verification as a distinct step from implementation, every time**, and ask what
  evidence proves the change worked, not just that it shipped. This is the same discipline you
  already apply to a CAPA's effectiveness check — apply it here too, on its own shorter clock.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA argues that 21 CFR Part 606 requires Lakeshore to run a formal change-control process before revising a controlled procedure. True or false?

False, as worded. Part 606's own text never uses the phrase "change control." What it does
require, in 606.100(b), is that written procedures be established, *maintained*, and kept
available where they're used — a standing obligation that any change has to respect, but the
regulation doesn't spell out a request-assess-approve-implement-verify methodology for getting
there. That structured process is AABB's Quality Systems Framework, under the Process Control
QSE — binding on Lakeshore through accreditation, not through the CFR's own words. Tell your
CIO: the law requires the procedure to stay correct and available; AABB's Standards supply the
disciplined process that proves it stayed that way through every revision.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Your QA wants to email the new distribution list directly to site leads today and treat the CAPA's fix as closed once everyone's replied. Is that acceptable?

No. That approach has no documented request, no impact and risk assessment, no named approver
with authority over the outcome, and no planned verification — it's a well-intentioned fix
implemented outside change control entirely. On paper, an uncontrolled change to a
document-control process is indistinguishable from the same kind of gap that produced the
original event: something changed, and there's no record showing anyone assessed it or
approved it first. The fix itself may be exactly right. It still has to go through a request,
an impact and risk assessment, a real approval from both Quality and IT, controlled
implementation with training and document issuance completed first, and a verification step
afterward — five separate, dated pieces of a record, not one email.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: The new distribution system goes live and every site lead's email shows as "delivered." Is the change verified?

No — that's implementation evidence, not verification evidence, and it's the same substitution
module 3 flagged for a CAPA's effectiveness check ("confirmed the binder was replaced" proves
implementation, not that the fix worked). "Delivered" only shows the message arrived; it
doesn't show a site lead actually signed and dated an acknowledgment, and it doesn't show the
system would catch a site that never responds. A real verification issues the next real
document revision through the new process and checks, with a dated record, that acknowledgments
actually came back and that a non-responding site gets flagged rather than quietly missed.
Delivery confirms the message went out. Verification confirms the process actually does its
job.
:::

## Where this goes next

This change is now approved, implemented, and verified — which means Lakeshore has a new,
current revision of the downtime SOP and a live distribution-and-acknowledgment process behind
it. But an approved change only gets you a document that's *supposed* to be controlled. Whether
it actually stays controlled — how it's drafted, reviewed, issued with an effective date,
trained on, periodically reviewed, and eventually retired without a stray copy surviving
somewhere the way the old revision survived at Brookfield — is document control's own job, the
subject of the next module, `document-control-and-records`.
